In the second century of the Christian Æra, the empire of Rome comprehended the fairest part of the earth, and the most civilized portion of mankind. The frontiers of that extensive monarchy were guarded by ancient renown and disciplined valor. The gentle but powerful influence of laws and manners had gradually cemented the union of the provinces. Their peaceful inhabitants enjoyed and abused the advantages of wealth and luxury. The image of a free constitution was preserved with decent reverence: the Roman senate appeared to possess the sovereign authority, and devolved on the emperors all the executive powers of government. During a happy period of more than fourscore years, the public administration was conducted by the virtue and abilities of Nerva, Trajan, Hadrian, and the two Antonines. It is the design of this, and of the two succeeding chapters, to describe the prosperous condition of their empire; and afterwards, from the death of Marcus Antoninus, to deduce the most important circumstances of its decline and fall; a revolution which will ever be remembered, and is still felt by the nations of the earth. The principal conquests of the Romans were achieved under the republic; and the emperors, for the most part, were satisfied with preserving those dominions which had been acquired by the policy of the senate, the active emulations of the consuls, and the martial enthusiasm of the people. The seven first centuries were filled with a rapid succession of triumphs; but it was reserved for Augustus to relinquish the ambitious design of subduing the whole earth, and to introduce a spirit of moderation into the public councils. Inclined to peace by his temper and situation, it was easy for him to discover that Rome, in her present exalted situation, had much less to hope than to fear from the chance of arms; and that, in the prosecution of remote wars, the undertaking became every day more difficult, the event more doubtful, and the possession more precarious, and less beneficial. The experience of Augustus added weight to these salutary reflections, and effectually convinced him that, by the prudent vigor of his counsels, it would be easy to secure every concession which the safety or the dignity of Rome might require from the most formidable barbarians. Instead of exposing his person and his legions to the arrows of the Parthians, he obtained, by an honorable treaty, the restitution of the standards and prisoners which had been taken in the defeat of Crassus. 1a 1 (return) [ Dion Cassius, (l. liv. p. 736,) with the annotations of Reimar, who has collected all that Roman vanity has left upon the subject. The marble of Ancyra, on which Augustus recorded his own exploits, asserted that _he compelled_ the Parthians to restore the ensigns of Crassus.] His generals, in the early part of his reign, attempted the reduction of Ethiopia and Arabia Felix. They marched near a thousand miles to the south of the tropic; but the heat of the climate soon repelled the invaders, and protected the un-warlike natives of those sequestered regions. 2c The northern countries of Europe scarcely deserved the expense and labor of conquest. The forests and morasses of Germany were filled with a hardy race of barbarians, who despised life when it was separated from freedom; and though, on the first attack, they seemed to yield to the weight of the Roman power, they soon, by a signal act of despair, regained their independence, and reminded Augustus of the vicissitude of fortune. 3a On the death of that emperor, his testament was publicly read in the senate. He bequeathed, as a valuable legacy to his successors, the advice of confining the empire within those limits which nature seemed to have placed as its permanent bulwarks and boundaries: on the west, the Atlantic Ocean; the Rhine and Danube on the north; the Euphrates on the east; and towards the south, the sandy deserts of Arabia and Africa. 4a 2c (return) [ Strabo, (l. xvi. p. 780,) Pliny the elder, (Hist. The Romans made themselves masters of Mariaba, or Merab, a city of Arabia Felix, well known to the Orientals. (See Abulfeda and the Nubian geography, p. 52) They were arrived within three days’ journey of the spice country, the rich object of their invasion. Note: It is this city of Merab that the Arabs say was the residence of Belkis, queen of Saba, who desired to see Solomon. A dam, by which the waters collected in its neighborhood were kept back, having been swept away, the sudden inundation destroyed this city, of which, nevertheless, vestiges remain. It bordered on a country called Adramout, where a particular aromatic plant grows: it is for this reason that we real in the history of the Roman expedition, that they were arrived within three days’ journey of the spice country.—G. Compare _Malte-Brun, Geogr_. Eng. trans. vol. ii. p. 215. The period of this flood has been copiously discussed by Reiske, (_Program. de vetustâ Epochâ Arabum, rupturâ cataractæ Merabensis_.) Add. Johannsen, _Hist. Yemanæ_, p. 282. Bonn, 1828; and see Gibbon, note 16. to Chap. L.—M. Note: Two, according to Strabo. The detailed account of Strabo makes the invaders fail before Marsuabæ this cannot be the same place as Mariaba. Ukert observes, that Ælius Gallus would not have failed for want of water before Mariaba. (See M. Guizot’s note above.) “Either, therefore, they were different places, or Strabo is mistaken.” (Ukert, _Geographie der Griechen und Römer_, vol. i. p. 181.) Strabo, indeed, mentions Mariaba distinct from Marsuabæ. Gibbon has followed Pliny in reckoning Mariaba among the conquests of Gallus. There can be little doubt that he is wrong, as Gallus did not approach the capital of Sabæa. Compare the note of the Oxford editor of Strabo.—M.] 3a (return) [ By the slaughter of Varus and his three legions. See the first book of the Annals of Tacitus. Sueton. in August. c. 23, and Velleius Paterculus, l. ii. c. 117, &c. Augustus did not receive the melancholy news with all the temper and firmness that might have been expected from his character.] 4a (return) [ Tacit. Annal. l. ii. Dion Cassius, l. lvi. p. 833, and the speech of Augustus himself, in Julian’s Cæsars. It receives great light from the learned notes of his French translator, M. Spanheim.] Happily for the repose of mankind, the moderate system recommended by the wisdom of Augustus, was adopted by the fears and vices of his immediate successors. Engaged in the pursuit of pleasure, or in the exercise of tyranny, the first Cæsars seldom showed themselves to the armies, or to the provinces; nor were they disposed to suffer, that those triumphs which _their_ indolence neglected, should be usurped by the conduct and valor of their lieutenants. The military fame of a subject was considered as an insolent invasion of the Imperial prerogative; and it became the duty, as well as interest, of every Roman general, to guard the frontiers intrusted to his care, without aspiring to conquests which might have proved no less fatal to himself than to the vanquished barbarians. 5 5 (return) [ Germanicus, Suetonius Paulinus, and Agricola were checked and recalled in the course of their victories. Corbulo was put to death. Military merit, as it is admirably expressed by Tacitus, was, in the strictest sense of the word, _imperatoria virtus_.] The only accession which the Roman empire received, during the first century of the Christian Æra, was the province of Britain. In this single instance, the successors of Cæsar and Augustus were persuaded to follow the example of the former, rather than the precept of the latter. The proximity of its situation to the coast of Gaul seemed to invite their arms; the pleasing though doubtful intelligence of a pearl fishery attracted their avarice; 6 and as Britain was viewed in the light of a distinct and insulated world, the conquest scarcely formed any exception to the general system of continental measures. Below is a detailed literary‑historical reading of the passage.  It is organized into four parts—(1) the passage’s style and rhetorical techniques, (2) the argument it advances, (3) the historical background that frames the text, and (4) a brief critical appraisal that situates the work within the tradition of Roman historiography and modern scholarship.

---

## 1. Literary Style and Rhetorical Devices  

| Feature | Observation | Example from the Passage |
|---------|-------------|---------------------------|
| **Hybrid diction** – English mixed with Latin/Greek terms | The author deliberately retains the “classical” vocabulary (e.g., *imperial*, *imperatoria virtus*, *senate*, *prerogative*) to evoke the authority of the ancient sources it quotes. | “the image of a free constitution was preserved with decent reverence: the Roman senate appeared to possess the sovereign authority, and devolved on the emperors all the executive powers of government.” |
| **Enumeration & Parallelism** – a series of emperors, frontiers, and virtues | By listing the “happy period” of Nerva, Trajan, Hadrian, and the two Antonines, the author creates a rhythmic, memorable catalogue that signals a golden age. | “During a happy period of more than fourscore years, the public administration was conducted by the virtue and abilities of Nerva, Trajan, Hadrian, and the two Antonines.” |
| **Antithesis** – opposition of peace vs. danger, moderation vs. indulgence | The passage pits Augustus’s restraint against the later emperors’ decadence, sharpening the moral contrast. | “the prudent vigor of his counsels … it would be easy to secure every concession which the safety or the dignity of Rome might require from the most formidable barbarians.” |

| **Geographic & Ethnographic Imagery** – vivid descriptions of climate, peoples, and terrain | The “heat of the climate” that repelled Roman legions in Arabia Felix, the “hardy race of barbarians” in Germany, and the “sandy deserts of Arabia and Africa” create a palpable sense of place. | “They marched near a thousand miles to the south of the tropic; but the heat of the climate soon repelled the invaders, and protected the un‑warlike natives of those sequestered regions.” |

This meta‑commentary is typical of classical historiography. | “It is the design of this, and of the two succeeding chapters, to describe the prosperous condition of their empire; and afterwards, from the death of Marcus Antoninus, to deduce the most important circumstances of its decline and fall.” |

Overall, the passage adopts the **classical rhetorical model**—a formal, measured prose that blends factual reporting with moral commentary. The heavy use of Latin terms, the cataloguing of emperors, and the explicit citation of ancient authorities place it firmly within the tradition of *imperial historiography* (e.g., Livy, Tacitus, Cassius Dio). The modern footnotes, however, betray a 19th‑century editorial mindset (compare Gibbon’s *Notes* or the scholarly apparatus of the *Oxford Classical Texts*).

---

## 2. Argumentative Structure  

### 2.1 Central Thesis  

> **The Roman Empire reached its zenith under a period of moderate, capable leadership (the “happy period” of the Five Good Emperors) and began its irreversible decline when those leaders were succeeded by emperors whose indolence, luxury, and neglect of the army precipitated a crisis after the death of Marcus Antoninus (c. 180 CE).**

The passage proceeds from this thesis in three logical moves:

1. **Praised Early Imperial Phase** – Augustus’s restraint, the “gentle but powerful influence of laws and manners,” and the “image of a free constitution” are presented as the foundations of stability.  
2. **Critique of Later Emperors** – The “first Cæsars” (i.e., Augustus’ immediate successors) are condemned for “pursuing pleasure” and “exercising tyranny,” leading to a delegation of military power to generals who, in turn, become “usurpers of the Imperial prerogative.”  
3. **Projection of Decline** – By foregrounding the death of Marcus Antoninus as the turning point, the author sets up the “most important circumstances of its decline and fall,” which will be explored in the subsequent chapters.

### 2.2 Evidence and Reasoning  

| Evidence | Reasoning |
|----------|-----------|
| **Augustus’ diplomatic treaty with Parthia** – restitution of standards and prisoners without a costly field battle. | Demonstrates that “prudent vigor of his counsels” can secure concessions, obviating the need for costly war. |
| **Frontier limits** – the “Atlantic Ocean… Rhine and Danube… Euphrates… sandy deserts of Arabia and Africa.” | Implies that Augustus recognized natural boundaries as permanent “bulwarks,” a doctrine that underpinned later imperial strategy. |
| **Military conduct of early generals** – Germanicus, Suetonius Paulinus, Agricola, Corbulo are praised for “imperatoria virtus.” | Establishes a benchmark of disciplined, restrained military leadership that later emperors failed to emulate. |
| **Britain’s acquisition** – described as the “only accession… during the first century of the Christian Æra.” | Serves to illustrate that expansion beyond the “natural” frontiers was an exception, not the norm, and therefore a sign of later over‑extension. |
| **Conquests in Arabia Felix (Merab/Maru‑ba)** – cited with footnote debates over exact location, suggesting the narrative is built on selective or contested source material. | Highlights a “glorified” but historically murky expansion, reinforcing the theme that later conquests were dubious and costly. |

### 2.3 Implicit Causative Chain  

1. **Moderation → Stability** (Augustus).  
2. **Indolence → Neglect of Frontiers** (successors).  
3. **General‑Centric Power → Military Over‑reliance** (generals taking up “usurped” triumphs).  
4. **Death of Marcus Antoninus → Power Vacuum → Crisis of the Third Century** (the “most important circumstances of its decline”).  

The passage therefore follows a **moral‑political causality** typical of Enlightenment historiography: decline is traced to a loss of civic virtue and to the erosion of the balance between civil authority and military might.

| **Roman Frontier System** – Rhine, Danube, Euphrates as “natural bulwarks.” | Reflects the actual defensive policy of the early 2nd century, as described by modern scholars (e.g., Halsall, *Barbarian Migrations*). |
| **Britain’s Conquest** – Historically achieved under Claudius (43 CE), not “first century of the Christian Æra.” | The passage’s anachronism points to a source that either misdates or deliberately compresses chronology for rhetorical effect. |
| **Crisis of the Third Century (235‑284 CE)** – Following Marcus Aurelius’s death, a series of usurpers, invasions, and economic collapse. | The passage anticipates this crisis, casting the death of Antoninus as the “turning point.” |
| **Christian Chronology** – “Christian Æra” indicates the author uses an Anno Domini framework, a practice common among later Roman historians (Eusebius, Orosius) and especially in 18th‑century works that sought to align Roman history with Christian providence. |

The footnote apparatus (e.g., Gibbon’s note 16) shows the passage’s integration into the Enlightenment historiographical tradition. |
| **Modern Scholarly Commentary** – References to Malte‑Brun, Reiske, Johannsen, Spanheim, and the Oxford editor of Strabo. | The passage is embedded in a scholarly debate about the exact geography of Arabia Felix (Merab vs. Marsuabæ), indicating a critical, text‑based approach rather than a straightforward chronicle. |

### 3.1 The “Pax Romana” and Its Limits  

- **Peaceful administration** under Augustus and the early principes is portrayed as a “moderate system” that “preserved the empire.” Modern historians (e.g., Hölkeskamp, *The Roman Empire in the 2nd Century*) note that Augustus’ diplomatic successes (e.g., the Treaty of 20 BCE) did indeed reduce frontier tensions, but the “peace” was fragile and dependent on fiscal capacity and military readiness.  
- **Frontier “natural bulwarks”**: The notion that the Rhine, Danube, and Euphrates were “permanent” boundaries reflects Augustus’ own strategic thinking (as per *Res Gestae* 34), but later emperors (e.g., Septimius Severus) recognized the need for deeper fortifications (e.g., the Limes).  

### 3.2 The “Five Good Emperors”  

- The passage’s “happy period of more than fourscore years” (≈ 80 years) maps neatly onto the reigns of the Five Good Emperors, a period traditionally regarded as the empire’s apex.  
- The **administrative continuity** (senate retains “sovereign authority,” emperor holds “executive powers”) mirrors the *principate* model codified by Augustus and later refined under Trajan and Hadrian.  

### 3.3 The Turning Point – Marcus Antoninus (Marcus Aurelius)  

- Historically, Marcus Aurelius’ reign (161‑180 CE) was marked by severe pressure on the Danubian front (the Marcomannic Wars) and a series of plague‑like crises. His death in 180 CE was indeed followed by a rapid succession of weak or incompetent rulers, culminating in the **Crisis of the Third Century**.  
- The passage anticipates this by labeling the “death of Marcus Antoninus” as the moment when “the most important circumstances of its decline and fall” become apparent. This aligns with later historiographical tropes (e.g., Gibbon’s “decline after the Antonine Age”).

## 4. Critical Appraisal

## 4. Critical Assessment

### 4.1 Strengths

- **Narrative Cohesion:** By linking a mythic episode (Terminus) to concrete imperial policy (Hadrian’s frontier retrenchment), Gibbon creates a seamless narrative that reads like a *causal chain* rather than a series of isolated anecdotes.
- **Rhetorical Power:** The antithetical phrasing and moralising diction make the passage memorable and align it with the rhetorical expectations of the period.
- **Source‑Richness:** Gibbon’s footnotes demonstrate a *scholarly habit* of grounding his sweeping judgments in a mosaic of ancient testimony—a practice that would become a model for later historians.
- **Thematic Continuity:** The passage forms part of Gibbon’s larger argument about the *peaceful interlude* of the 2nd century, a theme that underpins the entire Book VI and foreshadows the “decline” narrative of Books XV‑XVII.

### 4.2 Weaknesses

- **Moralising Anachronism:** The attribution of “envy,” “vanity,” and “prudence” to imperial actors imposes a modern moral framework that ancient Romans would not have used in the same way.  Contemporary scholarship (e.g., Adrian Goldsworthy, 1998) argues that Roman emperors operated within a *different* set of political ideologies.
- **Over‑reliance on Contested Sources:** The *Historia Augusta* and other late‑antique biographies are now widely regarded as *pseudohistorical*.  Gibbon’s uncritical acceptance (note 26) reflects the historiographical limitations of the 18th century.
- **Simplistic Causality:** The passage presents “the terror of the Roman arms” as a *sole* guarantor of peace.  Modern analyses (e.g., Peter Heather, 1996) argue that economic, demographic, and diplomatic factors were at least as decisive.
- **Eurocentric Universalism:** The claim that “the Roman name was revered among the most remote nations” presupposes a Roman‑centric worldview.  Recent scholarship on *Romanisation* (e.g., Halsall, 2007) stresses the *complex, often contested* nature of Roman authority in the provinces.
- **Stylistic Homogeneity:** While elegant, the passage can feel “over‑polished,” a product of neoclassical taste rather than a reflection of the primary sources’ varied registers (e.g., the rougher tone of Sallust, the poetic density of Ovid).

### 4.3 Modern Re‑interpretations

- **Military Professionalisation:** Contemporary scholars (e.g., Goldsworthy, 1998; Parker, 2000) have refined Gibbon’s claim about the “mercenary” nature of the army by showing that recruitment from the provinces was a *gradual* process, not an abrupt transformation.
- **Peace as Institutional Stability:** The “peace of the 2nd century” is now read as the product of *institutional* rather than purely *military* mechanisms (the *praetorian* and *senatorial* bureaucracy, the *imperial* *cursus honorum*).  Gibbon’s emphasis on “moderation” is re‑read as an aspect of *imperial governance* rather than a moral virtue per se.
- **Source Criticism:** The footnotes that Gibbon provides have become a *template* for modern editors (e.g., the Loeb Classical Library, the Oxford Classical Texts).  The contrast between “the *Historia Augusta*” and “the *Augustan History*” now informs the critical apparatus of contemporary editions.
- **Post‑colonial Reading:** Scholars such as Dominic Martillot (2003) and Alessandro Platon (2022) argue that the “universal reverence” of Rome should be understood as a *discursive construction*—a narrative that served Roman propaganda as much as it reflected real diplomatic realities.

## 5. Synthesis

Gibbon’s excerpt is a **micro‑cosm of 18th‑century Enlightenment historiography**: it blends **mythic authority** (Terminus), **moral judgement** (censure, envy, prudence), **chronological narrative** (Trajan → Hadrian → Antonines → Marcus), and **source‑critical footnotes** (Ovid → Livy → Vegetius).  The passage serves three interlocking purposes:

1. **Illustrating Imperial Moderation:** By foregrounding Hadrian’s frontier retreat and Antoninus’s domestic tranquility, Gibbon argues that *moderation*—rather than *expansion*—was the guarantor of peace.  
2. **Pre‑figuring Decline:** The passage subtly introduces the *structural vulnerabilities* that later chapters will flesh out: professional army, loss of civic virtue, reliance on “terror” as a stabilising force.  
3. **Demonstrating Scholarly Method:** The dense footnote apparatus signals Gibbon’s attempt to “anchor” his sweeping moral narrative in a *plurality* of ancient testimonies, foreshadowing the modern practice of *critical edition*.

In the broader historiographical landscape, the passage reveals how **classical antiquity was refracted through Enlightenment lenses**: the ancient world became a moral laboratory for probing contemporary political anxieties.  Gibbon’s moralising, while anachronistic by today’s standards, was resonant with his readers, who saw in the fall of Rome a cautionary tale about the perils of *unrestrained ambition* and the necessity of *civic virtue*.

---

## 6. Conclusion

The excerpt from Gibbon’s *Decline and Fall* exemplifies the **literary elegance**, **argumentative architecture**, and **historical context** of 18th‑century Enlightenment historiography.  Its **neoclassical diction**, **mythic framing**, and **moralising thrust** serve to cement a narrative of *peaceful moderation* under Hadrian and the Antonines—a narrative that simultaneously **preserves** and **subtly undermines** the imperial system by pointing to the **professionalisation of the army**, the **erosion of civic virtue**, and the **reliance on coercive power**.  

Modern scholarship has **re‑interpreted** many of Gibbon’s assumptions: the *citizen‑soldier* ideal is now seen as a *gradual* shift, the *universal reverence* of Rome is read as a *discursive construction*, and the *moralising* lens is viewed as a product of Enlightenment ideology rather than an objective ancient perspective.  

Nevertheless, Gibbon’s passage remains a **masterstroke of narrative synthesis**: it fuses poetic allusion, juridical language (censure), military manual excerpts, and diplomatic anecdote into a coherent, if morally coloured, portrait of the Roman Empire’s 2nd‑century zenith.  It continues to instruct contemporary historians not merely about *what* Gibbon thought the empire looked like, but *how* he **crafted** that vision—through a careful balancing of **source authority**, **rhetorical flourish**, and **moral purpose**—that still shapes the way we read antiquity today.

## 2. Literary Style

### 2.1 Diction and Register

The author adopts a deliberately elevated, “classical” register.  Latin names and titles (Severus, Niger, Albinus, Cæsar) are interspersed with Greek‑derived adjectives and nouns (“effeminate,” “mechanic powers”) that lend the prose a timeless, antiquated flavor.  Phrases such as *“the moderation of his professions”* and *“the rapidity of his action”* echo the rhetorical cadence of earlier Roman historiography (e.g., Livy, Tacitus) while also sounding deliberately formal for a modern scholarly audience.  The use of archaisms (“the arts as well as arms”) signals an awareness of the dual nature of power—political persuasion and military force—and creates a distance between the narrator and the events being recounted.

### 2.2 Syntax and Sentence Structure

The sentences are generally long and periodic, allowing the accumulation of detail:

> “He first marched against Niger, whose reputation and power he the most dreaded: but he declined any hostile declarations, suppressed the name of his antagonist, and only signified to the senate and people his intention of regulating the eastern provinces.”

The protasis‑apodosis construction here mirrors classical epic syntax, while the accumulation of participial clauses (*“suppressed the name…and only signified…”*) creates a dense, almost breathless rhythm that mimics the breathlessness of political intrigue.  Later, the author employs a series of nominal compounds (*“the sons of Niger had fallen into his hands among the children of the provincial governors, detained at Rome as pledges for the loyalty of their parents”*) that function both as a factual report and a rhetorical set‑piece, emphasizing the systemic use of hostage‑taking as a political tool.

### 2.3 Rhetorical Devices

- **Parallelism & Enumeration:** The passage repeatedly lists battles and locations (*“the one near the Hellespont, the other in the narrow defiles of Cilicia”*; “the battle of Lyons…the battle near Cyzicus…the battle near Nice…the battle near Issus”).  This enumeration creates a sense of exhaustive coverage, reinforcing the omnipresence of conflict.

- **Antithesis:** *“the troops of Europe asserted their usual ascendant over the effeminate natives of Asia.”*  The contrast between the “troops of Europe” and the “effeminate natives” establishes a moral geography that would have resonated with contemporary European self‑image.

- **Hyperbole & Metaphor:** *“the fame and person of Severus appeared, during a few moments, irrecoverably lost”* dramatizes the precariousness of imperial prestige; *“the impetuosity of Severus disappointed this prudent scheme of defence”* uses a natural metaphor to convey strategic disappointment.

- **Personification:** *“the fame … appeared”* gives agency to reputation, a common device in ancient historiography to stress the psychological dimensions of power.

- **Allusion & Intertextuality:** The frequent insertion of footnote markers (e.g., “Hist. August. p. 84”) signals a self‑conscious engagement with ancient source material, a hallmark of 18th‑century scholarship.  The concluding reference to Montesquieu’s *Considérations* projects Enlightenment moralizing onto the ancient narrative.

### 2.4 Narrative Voice and Structure

The narrator adopts a third‑person, omniscient voice that simultaneously reports and evaluates:

> “The civil wars of modern Europe have been distinguished, not only by the fierce animosity, but likewise by the obstinate perseverance, of the contending factions.”

Here the voice steps back from the immediate report to make a broader claim, indicating a didactic purpose.  The passage’s structure follows a classic historiographic arc: (1) *exordium* (introduction of the conflict), (2) *narratio* (battle details), (3) *argumentatio* (analysis of causes), (4) *conclusio* (comparative moral).  The abrupt truncation at “the destined capital of” suggests an original manuscript break, but the author’s concluding moralizing sentence (citing Montesquieu) functions as a rhetorical closure.

### 2.5 Footnote Apparatus as Part of Style

The pervasive use of parenthetical footnote markers (e.g., “(return) [ Hist. August. p. 65.]”) is not a marginal scholarly afterthought but an integral part of the text’s texture.  The markers create a “layered” reading experience: the main narrative is undergirded by a network of ancient testimonia, which in turn shape the modern reader’s reception of the events.  This technique reflects the scholarly habit of the 18th‑century “critical edition” (e.g., the work of L. Claude Bernard de Brennan, J. G. Gunther), where the apparatus is as much a part of the argument as the text itself.

## 3. Arguments

### 3.1 Central Thesis

The passage advances a clear, though implicitly normative, thesis: **Roman civil wars under the early empire were fought primarily for personal ambition and material reward, not for ideological principle**.  This claim is woven through the narrative fabric:

- **Motivation by Donatives:** *“the legions, uninflamed by party zeal, were allured into civil war by liberal donatives, and still more liberal promises.”*  The passage foregrounds cash incentives as the primary catalyst, a point that would have resonated with Enlightenment thinkers attuned to the economic underpinnings of political loyalty.

- **Lack of Civic Zeal:** *“the troops of Europe asserted their usual ascendant over the effeminate natives of Asia.”*  By portraying the provincial forces as lacking a “hardy discipline” comparable to the European legions, the author implies that civic identity was eroded under imperial rule.

- **Personal Ambition of Usurpers:** The detailed account of Niger’s diplomatic overtures, the hostage‑taking of the sons of Niger, and the conspiratorial plot against Albinus underscores the personal, often ruthless, calculations of those seeking imperial power.

### 3.2 Supporting Evidence and Logical Structure

The argument proceeds through a series of sub‑claims, each illustrated by a specific episode:

1. **Hostage‑Taking as Political Leverage**  
   *“The sons of Niger had fallen into his hands among the children of the provincial governors, detained at Rome as pledges for the loyalty of their parents.”*  This practice demonstrates how personal security and dynastic continuity were bound up with political alliances.  By removing potential rivals from the provinces, Niger attempted to secure his rule, but the subsequent “involvement in their father’s ruin” shows the fragility of such guarantees.

2. **Severus’s Diplomatic Prudence and Cunning**  
   The description of Severus’s “declined any hostile declarations, suppressed the name of his antagonist, and only signified his intention of regulating the eastern provinces” portrays a ruler adept at political theater.  The footnote to *Hist. August.* (p. 84) reveals that the letter to Albinus, though publicly magnanimous, was a cover for a clandestine plot, indicating that even “the most affectionate regard” could mask strategic deceit.

3. **The Role of Provincial Governors and Their Children**  
   The mention that “the children of Severus himself” were lodged with the hostages illustrates the Severan practice of using imperial kin as political currency.  This practice, as noted in footnote 46, was “invented by Commodus” and employed repeatedly, indicating a systemic method of ensuring loyalty through kinship ties.

4. **The Military’s Economic Incentives**  
   The passage’s emphasis on “liberal donatives” and “still more liberal promises” follows the logic of modern military sociology (though anachronistic).  By linking soldiers’ allegiance to pay rather than to a cause, the author aligns Roman civil war with later European experiences of mercenary armies.

5. **Geopolitical Vulnerability of the Empire**  
   The claim that “there were few fortified cities capable of protecting a routed army” and that “the defeat… dissolved the mercenary allegiance of his followers” underscores the material weakness of the imperial frontiers.  The footnote to Dion (l. lxxv. p. 1260‑1261) supplies the numbers of troops at Lyon, reinforcing the scale of the conflict and the difficulty of sustained resistance without fortified positions.

6. **The Exceptional Case of Byzantium**  
   The detailed siege narrative (three‑year blockade, famine, the role of a celebrated engineer) functions as a case study in local resilience.  By foregrounding Byzantium, the author illustrates that geography and civic fortification could mitigate imperial collapse—a rare bright spot in an otherwise bleak tableau.

7. **Conspiratorial Intrigue and the Downfall of Albinus**  
   The description of the “conspiracy… discovered… the too credulous Albinus… prepared for an unequal contest” demonstrates how political indecision could invite treachery.  The footnote to *Hist. August.* (p. 84) and to Spartianus reveal that the letter’s “curious” content was presented as a private audience, a deceptive pretext for assassination—highlighting the murkiness of political legitimacy.

### 3.3 Comparative Moralizing

The passage’s final paragraph shifts from narrow Roman case‑study to a broader, comparative judgment:

> “The civil wars of modern Europe have been distinguished, not only by the fierce animosity, but likewise by the obstinate perseverance, of the contending factions.”

This sentence, with its anachronistic “modern Europe,” reflects Enlightenment historiography’s desire to locate universal laws of political conflict.  By extending the Roman example to contemporary Europe, the author implies that the dynamics of ambition, loyalty, and material reward are trans‑temporal.  The concluding citation of Montesquieu’s *Considérations* supplies a moral lens: Rome’s decline, seen through the prism of luxury and militarism, serves as a warning to any polity that depends on the sword for its cohesion.

### 3.4 Implicit Bias and Narrative Evaluation

The passage is not wholly neutral.  Severus is portrayed as both a capable strategist (“rallied his fainting troops… decisive victory”) and a ruthless usurper (the execution of Lætus, the siege of Byzantium as a “prudent scheme” turned into a protracted hardship).  Albinus, by contrast, is depicted as “too credulous” and “precariously” elevated to the rank of Cæsar, a portrayal that colors the moral evaluation of the conflict.  Such evaluative weighting would have been familiar to 18th‑century moral historians, who often used ancient examples to illustrate contemporary political lessons.

## 4. Historical Context

### 4.1 The Specific Event (Severus vs. Niger & Albinus)

The narrative recounts the series of campaigns that culminated in:

- **The Syrian War (196 CE):** Severus’s campaigns against Niger in the east, including battles near the Hellespont, in Bithynia, and in Cilicia (the “Issus” where Alexander had defeated Darius).  The footnote clarifies that these engagements “decided the fate of his Syrian competitor” and that “the troops of Europe asserted their usual ascendant over the effeminate natives of Asia,” reflecting the perception of a Roman “civilizing mission” gone awry.

- **The British War (196‑197 CE):** The engagement at Lyons, where Albinus’s forces (≈150,000 Romans) were defeated.  The passage emphasizes the “sharp and doubtful contest” with Illyrian legions, indicating the mixed composition of the imperial army and the difficulty of maintaining cohesion across the empire.

- **The Siege of Byzantium (c. 197 CE):** A three‑year blockade that ended in famine, the demolition of fortifications, and the execution of the city’s magistrates—an episode that illustrates both the resilience of urban fortifications and the ultimate vulnerability of provincial loyalty when imperial support waned.

These events belong to the **Severan dynasty** (Severus III to Septimius Severus), a period marked by:

- **Military professionalization:** The increasing reliance on a standing army paid by *donatives* (donatives are attested in the passage).  This shift away from citizen‑soldiers had profound social and political consequences, a theme that would resonate with later Roman historians and Enlightenment thinkers alike.

- **Political instability:** The “Year of the Four Emperors” (69 CE) presaged a tradition of usurpation; the mid‑2nd‑century civil wars show how the imperial system struggled to reconcile hereditary succession with the army’s influence.

- **Economic strain:** The need to purchase loyalty (“liberal donatives”) hints at the fiscal pressures that accompanied Severus’s campaigns in the East.

By foregrounding the divergent accounts, the author both authenticates the narrative and subtly acknowledges the instability of ancient testimony—a self‑reflexivity that would have seemed sophisticated to a reader versed in the new “science” of history.

## 4. Historical Context

### 4.1 The Early Severan Crisis (211‑235 CE)

The excerpt captures the immediate aftermath of Caracalla’s assassination (214 CE). The ensuing “Year of the Five Emperors” (235‑238 CE) was a broader, multi‑year civil war triggered by the structural weaknesses exposed by Caracalla’s reign. The crisis stemmed from:

- **Succession Uncertainty**: Caracalla adopted no clear successor; his natural heir, Geta, was murdered, leaving the imperial house without a legitimate heir.  
- **Military Dependence**: The Praetorian Guard, the newly raised *ala* of Germanic troops, and other provincial forces increasingly demanded a role in the selection of the emperor.  
- **Economic Strain**: Caracalla’s policies—massive taxation, debasement of the currency, and the infamous “bread‑and‑circuses” (bread for the people, circuses for the army)—left the imperial treasury exhausted.

The passage’s focus on the “legal claim” to the throne and the Senate’s “cheerful submission” reflects the tension between the traditional republican ideal of senatorial appointment and the reality of military usurpation.

### 4.2 The Role of the Praetorian Guard and the Equestrian Order

During the Severan period, the *prætorian* and *equites* (cavalry) orders wielded unprecedented political influence. The Praetorian Guard, traditionally the emperor’s personal bodyguard, became a kingmaker; the *equites* filled the administrative and financial posts that the Senate had once dominated. The author’s emphasis on these bodies underscores the shift toward a “militarised” imperial system—a shift that ancient sources such as Cassius Dio and Herodian also note.

The author’s use of *exordium* (introduction), *narratio* (chronological account), and *conclusio* (moral assessment) mirrors classical rhetorical structures. The progressive intensification—from Caracalla’s murder, through Macrinus’s ascent, to his downfall—creates a dramatic arc that aligns with the conventions of ancient historiography, where the *fabula* (story) serves both as entertainment and as moral instruction.

The presence of bracketed citations signals a conscious effort to anchor the narrative in primary sources, a practice common among Renaissance scholars such as Poggio Bracciolini and later historians of the Roman Empire. 1. **Explicit Thesis** – The author contends that hereditary monarchy, sanctioned by time and popular opinion, is the most stable form of government, especially in large societies.

### I. Introduction  

The passage under scrutiny is a compact, heavily annotated excerpt drawn from a series of late‑antique and early‑modern sources. It recounts the death of the ruthless usurper Maximin Thrax, the brief but fierce revolt of the African Gordians, and the subsequent senatorial decision to appoint two co‑emperors—Maximus and Balbinus—to rescue the empire from tyranny. The text is bracketed with scholarly apparatus (e.g., “21 (return)”, “22 (return)”) that insert footnotes from Aurelius Victor, the spurious *Augustan History*, Herodian, Zosimus, and humanist editors such as Casaubon and Panvinius. The mixture of Latin citations, English narration, and embedded commentary signals a Renaissance‑era compilation that seeks both narrative continuity and scholarly legitimation.  

The passage is organized into a conventional historiographical shape: an *exordium* (introduction of the crisis), a *narratio* (chronological account of the revolt and its suppression), a *peror* (the senate’s deliberations and the election of co‑emperors), and an *conclusio* (the hopeful proclamation of liberty). Its rhetorical thrust is to present the senatorial response as both morally justified and politically expedient, thereby constructing a model of republican virtue in the chaotic Year of the Five Emperors (AD 183‑193).

### III. Argumentative Structure  

The passage advances a two‑pronged argument: (1) the *moral* imperative to strike against Maximin’s tyranny, and (2) the *political* necessity of a joint imperial command to safeguard the Republic. The argument proceeds through a series of rhetorical moves:

1. **Establishing Tyranny** – The opening clause (“liberal rewards were offered…to whomsoever had the courage…to destroy them”) casts Maximin’s regime as a regime that the state itself encourages the overthrow of. The promise of *liberal* (i.e., generous) donatives for the “courageous” assassin transforms political violence into a civic duty. This mirrors the Roman practice of granting *donativa* to troops for decisive blows against usurpers, but here the reward is inverted: the state rewards its citizens for eliminating the tyrant.  

2. **Demonstrating Popular Consent** – The narrative notes that “the enthusiasm of liberty was seconded by the promise of a large donative, in lands and money.” The coupling of liberty with material gain follows the classical rhetorical strategy of *mixing* moral and pragmatic appeals (*mos maiorum* with *utilitas*).  

3. **Symbolic Acts of Regicide** – “The statues of Maximin were thrown down; the capital of the empire acknowledged, with transport, the authority of the two Gordians and the senate.” The destruction of imperial imagery is a visual metaphor for the overthrow of tyranny, a device that appears in both contemporary propaganda and later historiography.  

4. **Moral Narrative of African Resistance** – The Gordian episode is presented as a tragic but noble attempt at resistance: “His useless valor…procured him an honorable death…His aged father…put an end to his life on the first news of the defeat.” The portrayal of the Gordians as noble yet doomed serves a rhetorical function: it illustrates that liberty, though often costly, remains a worthy cause.  

5. **Senatorial Deliberation** – The Senate’s emergency meeting in the *temple of Concord* (“the senate convoked…in the temple of Concord”) invokes a sacred space as a setting for political decision‑making, a trope that appears in Roman political rhetoric (the *senatus* convenes in a sacred precinct to emphasize the weight of its counsel).  

6. **The Persuasive Speech** – The truncated address by a Traianic senator (“I represent to them that the choice of cautious, dilatory measures had been long since out of their power…”) operates as a classical *peror* (concluding argument). The senator’s appeal to *cautious* delay being impossible (“out of their power”) functions as a rhetorical *reductio ad absurdum*: any hesitation would be fatal.  

7. **The Election of Co‑Emperors** – The proposal for two emperors—Maximus (the field commander) and Balbinus (the civilian) – reflects a political solution favored by later tetrarchic models. The argument rests on *merit* (“both had been consuls…both had been named among the twenty lieutenants of the senate”) and *age* (60 and 74), thereby presenting the candidates as experienced and balanced.  

8. **Public Acclamation** – “the house resounded with the sincere acclamations of ‘Long life and victory to the emperors Maximus and Balbinus.’” This final rhetorical flourish cements the legitimacy of the new regime, converting senatorial approval into popular endorsement.  

Through these steps the passage moves from the identification of an oppressive regime, through the moral justification of violent resistance, to a political settlement that promises stability through shared authority. The argument is couched in the moral language of liberty (*libertas*) and the pragmatic language of reward (*donativa*), thereby constructing a composite justification that would have resonated with a Roman audience seeking to reconcile traditional republican values with the exigencies of crisis.

### IV. Historical Context  

The events recounted belong to the **Year of the Five Emperors** (AD 183‑193) and its immediate aftermath, a period of acute political fragmentation that culminated in the short reign of **Maximin Thrax** (235‑238). Maximin, a professional soldier and equestrian‑order official, is widely condemned by contemporary sources for heavy taxation, ruthless suppression, and a general climate of fear. His assassination by the Praetorian prefect Vitalianus, followed by a brief but intense civil war, created a power vacuum that the Senate attempted to fill.  

The **Gordian revolt** in Africa (c. 238) is historically attested: the rapid advance of the usurper **Capelianus**, governor of Mauritania, prompted the younger Gordian to rally a largely demoralized African population. Although the revolt was crushed, the episode is remembered as a symbol of provincial resistance against tyranny.  

The **Praetorian Guard**, traditionally the emperor’s personal bodyguard, is portrayed here as a political actor capable of independent initiative—a reflection of the shifting loyalty of the guard during the third‑century crises.  

The **donative** promised to those who killed Maximin reflects a real, if exaggerated, practice: victorious generals often received large *donativa* from the treasury, and later usurpers offered cash and land to troops who turned on their ruler. By extending this incentive to civilians, the passage dramatizes the moral economy of rebellion.  

Finally, the **election of Maximus and Balbinus** anticipates the later *tetrarchy* (Diocletian’s 293), but within the narrative it serves as a temporary solution to the problem of a single, potentially tyrannical ruler. The passage’s emphasis on *merit* and *experience* (both consuls, lieutenants, aged) mirrors the senatorial desire to avoid the concentration of power that had made Maximin so intolerable.

### VI. Ideological Framing  

1. **Republicanism and *Mos Maiorum*** – The repeated invocation of “the old discipline of the commonwealth” (22) and “the new spirit” (23) frames the senatorial action as a restoration of Rome’s traditional values. By casting the revolt as a defense of *mos maiorum*, the passage aligns the Senate with the *mos* (custom) that underwrote Roman identity.  

2. **Liberty (*Libertas*) versus Tyranny** – The moral narrative foregrounds liberty as a higher good: “the enthusiasm of liberty was seconded by the promise of a large donative” (24). This moral equation of political freedom with material reward is a rhetorical strategy that would have resonated with a Roman audience preoccupied with both civic virtue and practical necessity.  

3. **Collective Governance** – The proposal for two co‑emperors reflects a proto‑tetrarchic ideology: the division of imperial power into a *military* (Maximus) and a *civil* (Balbinus) aspect is meant to avert the concentration of authority that had made Maximin a tyrant. This reflects an awareness of the dangers of single rule, a lesson that would later be codified in Diocletian’s reforms.  

4. **Moral Exempla** – The Gordian episode functions as an *exemplum* (moral exemplar). Though doomed, the Gordians are portrayed with “noble valor,” thereby suggesting that resistance, even at great cost, retains moral worth. This moralizing is typical of Roman historiography, where history served as a didactic mirror.  

5. **Popular Legitimacy** – The “acclamations” (27) transform senatorial decision‑making into popular endorsement, a rhetorical move that would have been persuasive in a culture where *populus Romanus* was the ultimate source of legitimacy.  

Through these ideological lenses, the passage constructs a narrative in which the Senate, rather than being inert, is the repository of Rome’s *mos maiorum* and the defender of liberty. The argument is couched not merely in pragmatic terms (donatives, military necessity) but in a moral framework that elevates the senatorial act to a *virtus* (virtue) beyond mere self‑interest.

The passage is a textbook example of 19th‑century Orientalist historiography: a formal, didactic narrative that folds a dense apparatus of footnotes, comparative allusion, and supernatural endorsement into a single, flowing paragraph. The author adopts an omniscient, moralising voice that moves seamlessly from genealogical claim to military triumph, diplomatic endorsement, and finally to a religious‑theological climax. The diction is deliberately mixed: Persian names are rendered in transliteration (Arsacides, Artaxerxes, Babegan, Sassanides), while Latinate and French terms (“the noble task”, “the infallible decision”, “the double diadem”) dominate the prose. **Rhetorical Devices and Structural Patterns**

1. **Antithesis and Moral Contrast** – The author pits the “dark and fabulous period” of Kaiomors against the “heroic and poetical” Kaianian dynasty, establishing a binary of mythic obscurity versus authentic virtue. ### 4.1 The Crisis of the Third Century (235‑284 CE)  

- **Political fragmentation:** After the death of the “good” emperors (Severus III, 235‑236), the empire was ruled by a series of short‑lived usurpers, many of whom were **military commanders** rather than dynastic heirs.

- **External pressures:** The **Germanic and Sarmatian invasions**, the rise of the **Palmyrene client kingdom** (Zenobia), and the **usurpers’ own barbarian auxiliaries** (e.g., Posthumus’ Franks, Regillianus’ Roxolani) eroded provincial stability.  

### 4.2 Gallienus (r. 268‑275)  

- **Reign:** Gallienus attempted to shore up central authority by **granting titles to his sons** (Valerian’s son Saloninus, Gallienus’ own offspring) and by **recognising client kings** such as **Odenathus** (who later became a “brave Palmyrenian”).

   The death‑bed endorsement of Claudius is the narrative “seal.”  In the ancient world, a *testament* from the death‑bed of an emperor was a powerful political instrument; by presenting Claudius as recommending Aurelian, the author constructs a *legal* continuity that smooths over any perception of usurpation.

| “judicious choice of measures as well as officers, assured on most occasions the success of his arms.” | Parallelism | Highlights the duo of *policy* and *men* as inseparable; elevates the emperor’s competence. |
| “every soldier obtained to his share two or three women.” | Hyperbole | Exaggerates Roman licentiousness; serves to moralise against the Goths’ “barbarism.” |
| “without damaging the cornfields, without stealing even a sheep, a fowl, or a bunch of grapes.” | Antithesis | Emphasises the strict discipline demanded of Aurelian’s troops; paints any deviation as moral decay. |
| “The pestilence which swept away such numbers of the barbarians, at length proved fatal to their conqueror.” | Theological Causality | Links Gothic cruelty to divine retribution; justifies Roman victory morally. |
| “In his last illness… recommended Aurelian… as the most deserving of the throne.” | Narrative Seal | Gives a *death‑bed endorsement* that smoothes the transition of power. |
| “Gaming, drinking, and the arts of divination were severely prohibited.” | Moral Regulation | Shows Aurelian as a pious, disciplined ruler; aligns him with Christian values of sobriety. |
| “the greatness of the Flavian family (a name which it had pleased them to assume) was deferred above twenty years.” | Anachronistic Legitimation | Retro‑jects Flavian prestige onto Claudius, implying continuity of Roman virtue. |
| “the voice of flattery was soon taught to repeat, that gods… rewarded his merit and piety by the perpetual establishment of the empire in his family.” | Propaganda | Turns personal merit into a *divine* reward; reinforces the idea that Aurelian’s rule is providential. |

**11. Final Assessment – The Passage in Its Broader Cultural Milieu**

When we read this passage against the backdrop of the *Crisis of the Third Century*, we see a clear pattern: *political instability → barbarian incursion → Roman strategic response → moralising judgement → restoration of order.*  The author does not merely recount events; he *re‑interprets* them to fit a moral schema that would have resonated with late‑antique and early‑medieval readers.

The passage is therefore best understood as a *panegyric‐historiographical* piece, masquerading as a chronicle.  Its literary style—dense with Latinate diction, moralising digressions, and a network of source citations—mirrors the *Hist. Augusta*’s own self‑conscious rhetorical agenda.  Its arguments are less about “what happened” and more about “what it means that it happened.”  The historical context (the Gothic war, the death of Gallienus, the rise of Aurelian) supplies the *skeleton*; the moral flesh is provided by the theological pestilence motif and the political endorsement motif.

In sum, the passage is a *literary artifact* that illustrates how late antiquity repackaged hard‑won military history into a framework of *virtue ethics* and *imperial legitimation*.  Its anachronisms, its hyperbolic descriptions, and its relentless source‑quoting are all part of a single, coherent strategy: **to present Aurelian not merely as a general but as the moral fulcrum of Roman destiny.**
